summary: Cross-Sandbox Filesystem Access via Guest-Controlled Root Disk Journal
description:
### Impact

Microsandbox 0.7.8 for Windows contains a cross-sandbox filesystem isolation vulnerability. A workload running inside one sandbox can cause the host runtime to attach another sandbox's writable root disk after a restart, allowing unauthorized read and persistent write access to the target sandbox's filesystem.

The vulnerability occurs because the runtime exposes `runtime_dir` to the guest as the writable `/.msb` filesystem while storing the host-trusted `root-disk.json` journal in that same directory. The journal contains absolute host filesystem paths in `layers`, but its validation does not ensure that these paths remain within the current sandbox's storage directory. During startup, `recover_runtime_owned_root()` accepts the journal's layer paths and uses them to reconstruct the writable root disk, allowing guest-controlled data to influence which disk is attached.

This breaks the intended filesystem isolation between sandboxes and can expose application data, source code, configurations, and credentials. Exploitation requires knowledge of the target sandbox's name and that its disk is not in use when attached to the modified sandbox. No direct host filesystem access, administrative privileges, or shared volume is required.

### Technical References

- [Runtime directory mount](https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/blob/7b7b9dc89e9a1c77801918f7833c3381d1754579/crates/runtime/lib/runner/vm.rs#L2066-L2084)
- [External mount authorization storage](https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/blob/7b7b9dc89e9a1c77801918f7833c3381d1754579/crates/runtime/lib/checkpoint/external_mounts.rs#L27-L37)
- [RootDiskState journal structure](https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/blob/7b7b9dc89e9a1c77801918f7833c3381d1754579/crates/runtime/lib/checkpoint/disk.rs#L87-L104)
- [Insufficient journal path validation](https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/blob/7b7b9dc89e9a1c77801918f7833c3381d1754579/crates/runtime/lib/checkpoint/disk.rs#L691-L715)
- [recover_runtime_owned_root](https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/blob/7b7b9dc89e9a1c77801918f7833c3381d1754579/crates/runtime/lib/checkpoint/disk.rs#L847-L881)
- [Writable root-disk attachment](https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/blob/7b7b9dc89e9a1c77801918f7833c3381d1754579/crates/runtime/lib/runner/vm.rs#L1992-L2009)
- [Filesystem isolation documentation](https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/blob/main/docs/security/filesystem.mdx)

### PoC

A proof of concept was included in the original report by joaoviictorti but is not publicly available.

summary: Sandbox catalog database is created world-readable, exposing persisted secret and environment values to other local users
description:
### Summary

The local backend creates `$MSB_HOME/db/` with mode `0755` and `msb.db`, `msb.db-wal` and
`msb.db-shm` with mode `0644`. No mode is set explicitly, so the files get whatever the process
umask leaves (`022` on a default macOS or Linux login).

Every sandbox's full configuration is stored in that database. That includes:

- the real values of secrets supplied inline through an SDK, and
- the values of the sandbox's environment variables.

Any other local account that can traverse the path to `$MSB_HOME` can read these values with
`sqlite3` or `strings`. They stay readable until the sandbox is *removed* (stopping it does not
delete the row), and they remain in `msb.db-wal` after removal.

This is the same exposure class as GHSA-m8f5-rh7h-vgg3 (CVE-2026-61670), which took these values
out of world-readable process arguments. The same values are still readable by the same local
users: at rest, and for longer than the sandbox runs.

The documentation already says that raw SDK values persist in the host-side sandbox
configuration (`docs/sandboxes/secrets.mdx`, and "Where the values live" in
`docs/security/secrets.mdx`). This report is not about that persistence. It is about the
permissions the store is created with, and about what is left behind after a sandbox is removed.





Suggested: Medium, `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N` (6.5). This is the vector
assigned to GHSA-m8f5-rh7h-vgg3.

CWE-276 (Incorrect Default Permissions), CWE-312 (Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information).

## Versions and platform

- Observed: `msb 0.7.2` (CLI), and core `0.6.18` through an SDK binding.
- Read, not run: source at `v0.7.6` (the references above).
- Host: macOS 27.2 (26B5091g), Apple M3 Pro (arm64).

## Disclosure

Found during an audit of the downstream Ruby SDK `microsandbox-rb`. Not disclosed anywhere else.
I can test a fix. If you consider this hardening rather than a vulnerability, I'm happy to refile
it as a public issue.


### Details

References are to tag `v0.7.6`.

- `crates/db/lib/pool.rs:78-98`, `build_pool`: the pool is opened with
  `SqliteConnectOptions::new().filename(db_path).create_if_missing(create_if_missing).journal_mode(SqliteJournalMode::Wal)…`.
  SQLite creates the file `0644 & ~umask`, and the `-wal` and `-shm` files take the main file's
  mode.
- `sdk/rust/lib/backend/local/mod.rs:616`: `tokio::fs::create_dir_all(db_dir)` creates `db/`
  `0777 & ~umask`.
- The migration lock next to the database is created `0600` (see the listing below), so
  restrictive creation is already in use in this directory. The database itself was missed.
- What the rows contain:
  - Inline secret values. `crates/network/lib/model/config/builder.rs:641-648` documents that
    "an inline value is persisted verbatim in the sandbox spec"; `SecretEntry.value`
    (`packages/microsandbox-types/rust/lib/domain.rs:2362-2373`) is a serialized field.
  - Environment values (`pub env: Vec<EnvVar>` at `domain.rs:925`).
- Nothing sets `PRAGMA secure_delete`, and nothing truncates the WAL when a sandbox is removed.


### Proof of concept

`msb 0.7.2` on macOS 27.2 (26B5091g), Apple M3 Pro, `umask 022`, using an empty `MSB_HOME`:

```console
$ export MSB_HOME=/tmp/msb-poc          # empty directory
$ msb create public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:latest --name permpoc -e API_TOKEN=ENV-CANARY-7f3a91
$ ls -ld $MSB_HOME $MSB_HOME/db
drwxr-xr-x  /tmp/msb-poc
drwxr-xr-x  /tmp/msb-poc/db
$ ls -l $MSB_HOME/db
-rw-r--r--  msb.db
-rw-r--r--  msb.db-shm
-rw-r--r--  msb.db-wal
-rw-------  msb.db.migration.lock
$ sqlite3 $MSB_HOME/db/msb.db "select name, status, instr(config, 'ENV-CANARY-7f3a91') > 0 from sandbox"
permpoc|Running|1
$ msb stop permpoc && msb remove permpoc
   ✓ Stopped      permpoc
   ✓ Removed      permpoc
$ sqlite3 $MSB_HOME/db/msb.db "select count(*) from sandbox"
0
$ grep -a -c ENV-CANARY-7f3a91 $MSB_HOME/db/msb.db $MSB_HOME/db/msb.db-wal
msb.db:0
msb.db-wal:7
```

The row is gone, the value is still in the WAL, and every file involved is readable by other
users.

Inline secret values: I reproduced this on `0.6.18` through an SDK binding (the Ruby gem
`microsandbox-rb` 0.17.0, which embeds the same Rust core). A sandbox created with an inline
secret has the value at `network.secrets.secrets[0].value` in `sandbox.config`. The row, with the
value, is also left behind when `create` fails after the catalog insert (I triggered that with a
missing `libkrunfw`; the row stays as `Stopped`). I did not re-run the inline-secret case on
0.7.x; the code path is the one cited above.


### Impact

Who can read the values: any local account that can traverse to `$MSB_HOME`.

- With the default `~/.microsandbox`, that depends on the home directory's mode. On macOS the
  home directory is group-accessible to `staff`, which every local user belongs to (observed:
  `drwxr-x---`, group `staff`). On Linux it depends on the distribution's default.
- When `MSB_HOME` points at a shared location (a service account's state directory, a CI
  runner's workspace), nothing above the database restricts access.

What they get:

- API keys and tokens bound as inline secrets. These are the values secret injection exists to
  keep away from everything but the host process.
- Environment values, which commonly carry credentials.
- The rest of each sandbox's configuration.

How long: until the sandbox is removed, not until it stops; in WAL frames after removal; and in
any copy of the database. On a long-lived home I also see `msb.db.bak-<epoch>` files next to the
catalog, mode `0644`.

Not affected: values supplied as host environment references (the CLI's `--secret NAME@host`,
and the SDKs' environment-source forms). Only the reference is stored.

summary: Relative bind mount paths are re-resolved against the current directory when a sandbox restarts
description:
### Summary
Relative host paths given for bind mounts, for example `--mount-dir ./:/workspace`, were saved as written instead of being resolved to absolute paths when the sandbox was created. Each time the sandbox started, the path was resolved against the working directory of the process starting it. Restarting a sandbox from a different directory therefore mounted a different host directory than the one originally intended.

### Impact
A user who restarts an existing sandbox from another directory, such as their home directory, can unintentionally expose that directory to the sandbox. Code running inside the sandbox can then read its contents, and modify them if the mount is writable. This can expose credentials, keys, or other files the user never meant to share with the sandbox.

Exploitation requires a user to restart the sandbox from a different working directory. Code inside the sandbox cannot change the mount on its own. Access remains subject to the host user's file permissions, and read-only mounts limit the impact to disclosure. This is not a kernel or hypervisor escape.

### Affected configurations
The issue affects versions 0.3.0 through 0.7.5 when both of the following are true:

- a sandbox is created with a relative host path for a bind mount, through the CLI or an SDK
- the sandbox is later started from a different working directory

Sandboxes created with absolute host paths are not affected. Versions before 0.3.0 have not been assessed.

### Patches
Fixed in 0.7.6. Host paths are now resolved to absolute paths when a sandbox is created, so later restarts use the original directory regardless of the working directory.

Upgrading does not change existing sandboxes. A sandbox created on an affected version with a relative path keeps its saved relative path and its previous behavior. Recreate those sandboxes after upgrading, or recreate them with absolute paths.

### Workarounds
Use absolute host paths when creating sandboxes. For an existing sandbox with saved relative paths, restart it only from its original working directory and check which host directories are mounted before running untrusted code.

### References
- https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/issues/1617

summary: Microsandbox hostname allowlist bypass via mismatched HTTP Host/:authority
description:
## Summary

Microsandbox hostname-based egress allow rules could be bypassed when the hostname used to authorize a connection did not match the later HTTP request authority.

For plaintext HTTP, a sandbox could connect through an allowed hostname and send a different `Host` header. For HTTPS with TLS interception disabled or bypassed, Microsandbox could observe DNS/SNI and destination IP state, but could not inspect the encrypted `Host` / `:authority` value used by the upstream service after TLS was established.

This affects sandboxes that rely on hostname allowlists as an egress security boundary, especially deny-by-default configurations running untrusted code.

## Impact

An attacker who can execute code inside a sandbox may be able to reach an unlisted destination through compatible shared infrastructure, such as a CDN, reverse proxy, or multi-tenant service edge that routes requests by HTTP `Host` or HTTP/2 `:authority`.

This can allow exfiltration of secrets, source code, user/model data, or other data available to the sandboxed process. It can also allow payload download or command-and-control traffic despite a hostname allowlist.

This is not a host escape and does not by itself grant code execution outside the sandbox.

## Affected configurations

The issue affects versions before 0.6.18 when all of the following are true:

- the sandbox uses hostname-based egress allow rules, usually with default-deny egress;
- untrusted or attacker-controlled code can run inside the sandbox;
- the attacker can use compatible shared infrastructure where the connection hostname and request authority can differ.

Plaintext HTTP was affected before 0.6.18. HTTPS was affected when TLS interception was disabled or bypassed, because the encrypted request authority was not inspectable by Microsandbox.

Versions 0.6.18 through 0.7.2 include the HTTP fix and strict hostname policy support, but users who rely on HTTPS hostname allowlists without TLS interception should enable strict mode. Version 0.7.3 enables strict hostname policy mode by default.

HTTPS authority validation when TLS interception is enabled was previously addressed in https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/pull/709.

## Patches

Upgrade to 0.6.18 or later.

- 0.6.18 fixed plaintext HTTP `Host` alignment and added strict hostname policy mode.
- 0.7.3 enables strict hostname policy mode by default, so hostname-only allows fail closed when Microsandbox cannot inspect request authority.

## Workarounds

For 0.6.18 through 0.7.2, enable strict hostname policy mode for sandboxes that rely on HTTPS hostname allowlists without TLS interception:

- CLI: `--net-strict`
- Config/SDKs: `network.strict = true`

Alternatively, enable TLS interception for HTTPS hostname allowlists where request authority must be verified.

If a sandbox already allows broad outbound internet access, the practical impact of this issue is reduced because hostname allowlists are not being used as the primary egress boundary.

## References

- Plaintext HTTP fix and strict hostname policy support in 0.6.18: https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/releases/tag/v0.6.18
- Strict mode enabled by default in 0.7.3: https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/pull/1643
- v0.7.3 release: https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/releases/tag/v0.7.3
- TLS-intercepted HTTPS authority alignment: https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/pull/709

summary: Volume filesystem API writes outside the volume root when a path traverses through a component that does not exist (resolve_relative, lib/volume/fs.rs)
description:
### Summary

`VolumeFs`'s path guard can be bypassed. A relative path whose first component
does not exist keeps its `..` segments through `resolve_relative`, passes the
containment check, and is handed to the filesystem with the traversal intact, so
the write lands outside the volume it was addressed to. The same shape is
correctly refused when that component *does* exist — the guard works only for
paths it can resolve, and the caller chooses the path.

Verified on 0.6.15 and 0.6.16 (`resolve_relative` is byte-identical between
them). Earlier versions were not checked.

### Details

`resolve_relative`, `lib/volume/fs.rs:338`, reached by every volume filesystem
operation. Three steps, and the third undoes the first two:

1. `root.join(clean)` — `Path::join` does not normalise `..`.
2. When the joined path does not exist, it walks up to the deepest **existing**
   ancestor, canonicalises that, and re-joins the remainder — which still
   contains the `..` components.
3. `if !canonical.starts_with(&canon_root)` — `Path::starts_with` is a
   component-wise prefix test and does not normalise `..` either.

For `absent/../../escape.txt` nothing resolves until the walk reaches the volume
root, so the value tested is the original path re-joined onto the root. It does
literally begin with the root's components, the check passes, and the `..` are
still present when the path reaches `open()`.

**Suggested fix:** normalise the joined path lexically — resolve `.` and `..` as
text — before the containment test, and refuse anything that is not a proper
descendant. A lexical rule has no unresolvable-path case to get wrong, and doing
it before any filesystem call also avoids the symlink and TOCTOU questions that
canonicalisation invites.

**Platform note.** Every one of these paths is refused on native Windows and
accepted on Linux. On Unix, `exists()` through a missing component fails, so the
walk climbs to the root and the traversal survives; on Windows, `exists()`
normalises `..` lexically first, so the walk stops at a real ancestor outside the
root and `starts_with` correctly fails. Windows is protected by its path API
rather than by this code.

### PoC

Self-contained, public API only, no sandbox and no KVM.

```toml
[dependencies]
microsandbox = "0.6.16"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
```

```rust
use microsandbox::Volume;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let msb_home = std::env::var("MSB_HOME").expect("set MSB_HOME to a disposable dir");
    let vol = "poc-volume";
    let _ = Volume::remove(vol).await;
    Volume::builder(vol.to_string()).create().await?;
    let handle = Volume::get(vol).await?;

    // Control: the same shape through a component that DOES exist is refused.
    handle.fs().mkdir("real").await?;
    match handle.fs().write("real/../../control.txt", b"control".to_vec()).await {
        Err(e) => println!("through an existing component : REFUSED ({e})"),
        Ok(_)  => println!("through an existing component : allowed (unexpected)"),
    }

    // The bug.
    match handle.fs().write("absent/../../ESCAPED.txt", b"escaped\n".to_vec()).await {
        Ok(_)  => println!("through a missing  component : ALLOWED"),
        Err(e) => println!("through a missing  component : refused ({e})"),
    }

    let outside = std::path::Path::new(&msb_home).join("volumes").join("ESCAPED.txt");
    println!("OUTSIDE the volume {}: {}", outside.display(), outside.exists());
    Ok(())
}
```

```
$ MSB_HOME=/tmp/msb-poc-home cargo run
through an existing component : REFUSED (sandbox fs error: path traversal outside volume root)
through a missing  component : ALLOWED
OUTSIDE the volume /tmp/msb-poc-home/volumes/ESCAPED.txt: true
```

All write-side operations are affected — `write`, `write_stream`, `mkdir`,
`copy`, `rename` — verified individually.

**One trap when reproducing by hand:** the first call through a given missing
component *creates* it, so every later call through the same path resolves and is
correctly refused. Testing several operations against one path makes whichever
ran first look like the only affected one. Use a fresh component per case.

Environment: Ubuntu 24.04.4, Linux 6.18.44 x86_64, rustc 1.94.1, crate from
crates.io. Also reproduced inside a `debian-slim` container running as a non-root
uid.

### Impact

Any caller who can address one volume can write anywhere the microsandbox process
can write. From a volume root at `$MSB_HOME/volumes/<name>`:

- **two levels up → `$MSB_HOME/volumes/`** — every other volume. This is an
  isolation bypass between sandboxes: one volume's caller writes into another's,
  including volumes holding a different workload's working tree.
- **three → `$MSB_HOME`** — sandbox state, images, snapshots and the database.
- **beyond** — bounded only by the process's credentials. As a dedicated non-root
  user the writes stop at the first directory it cannot write (`EACCES`); as root
  they do not stop.

**What this is not:** a guest-to-host escape. A guest writing through a mounted
volume goes via the kernel and is unaffected. The exposure is to callers of the
host-side volume API — for an embedder, whatever it lets reach that API. We hit
it because our gateway exposes those operations over HTTP to API-key holders and
relied on this function to keep each caller inside the volume it named.

We also checked the **sandbox** filesystem API (`Sandbox::fs()`) and are
deliberately **not** reporting it: `..` climbs out of any directory there, but so
does a plain absolute path, because that API takes absolute guest paths and
confines nothing to a base. The traversal reaches nothing a direct write does
not. The volume API is the one making a containment promise.

On severity: `C:N` is measured rather than assumed. `AV` and `A` are judgement —
`AV:L` gives 8.4 and `A:L` gives 8.5, so the scoring choice moves the number and
not the urgency. Yours to set.
```

cwes.name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory

summary: NAT64 addresses can bypass network destination group policy
description:
## Summary

microsandbox's network policy engine classified destinations in NAT64 IPv6 prefixes only as IPv6 addresses. In NAT64-capable environments, a sandbox restricted to public egress could target an IPv6 NAT64 address whose embedded IPv4 address was private, loopback, link-local, or cloud metadata, and the destination could be treated as ordinary public IPv6 traffic.

## Impact

A sandbox workload with public-only egress policy could bypass destination group restrictions on networks that route the targeted NAT64 prefix. The highest-impact case is access to cloud metadata addresses such as `169.254.169.254` through the well-known NAT64 prefix `64:ff9b::/96`.

This affects network policy enforcement for translated IPv4 destinations, including private, loopback, link-local, and metadata IPv4 ranges.

## Affected versions

The DestinationGroup policy classifier is present in tagged releases starting at `0.3.13`. Releases from `0.3.13` through `0.7.4` are affected.

Standalone `msb` binaries from `v0.3.13` through `v0.7.4` are also affected. The issue is fixed in v0.7.5.

## Patched behavior

The fix classifies destinations in configured NAT64 `/96` prefixes by both their IPv6 address and the embedded IPv4 address. The well-known `64:ff9b::/96` prefix is enabled by default, and deployments can configure additional NAT64 `/96` prefixes when their environment routes them.

The fix does not try to automatically detect every possible NAT64 prefix. NAT64 prefixes can be deployment-specific, so arbitrary IPv6 ranges are not treated as embedded IPv4 unless they are the well-known prefix or are explicitly configured by the operator.

## Workarounds

Before upgrading, operators can reduce exposure by disabling sandbox networking for untrusted workloads or by blocking routed NAT64 prefixes at the host or network boundary. Environments that do not route NAT64 prefixes are not expected to be exploitable through the NAT64 vector.

## Credit

Reported by tonghuaroot.

summary: Egress allowlist bypass: Host/SNI check fails open on malformed HTTP/1 request lines
description:
### Summary
On intercepted TLS connections, microsandbox checks that the HTTP request authority matches the TLS SNI. This stops a sandbox from connecting to an allowed hostname and then addressing the request to a different backend behind it (domain fronting).

For HTTP/1, this check was skipped when the request line could not be parsed. A sandbox could send a malformed request line, for example one preceded by an empty line, that microsandbox passed through unchecked but a tolerant upstream server still accepted.

HTTP/2 was not affected.

### Impact
An attacker who can execute code inside a sandbox may be able to reach an unlisted backend through an allowed hostname, when that hostname is served by shared infrastructure that routes requests by HTTP `Host`, such as a CDN, reverse proxy, or multi-tenant platform. This bypasses hostname-based egress allow rules for intercepted HTTPS traffic.

Where a secret is configured for the allowed host, the secret could also be substituted into a request carrying a different `Host`. The sandbox does not learn the secret value and the connection still terminates at the allowed host's server, so disclosure depends on the same shared-infrastructure condition.

Destinations that do not route by `Host` are not exploitable this way. DNS pinning and the filtering of private, loopback, link-local, and metadata addresses are not affected. This is not a host escape.

### Affected configurations
The issue affects versions 0.5.3 through 0.6.8 when all of the following are true:

- TLS interception is enabled for the destination
- untrusted or attacker-controlled code can run inside the sandbox
- an allowed hostname is served by infrastructure where the connection hostname and the HTTP/1 `Host` can differ

It applies whether or not secrets are configured.

### Patches
Fixed in 0.6.9. HTTP/1 requests on intercepted connections that cannot be parsed are now blocked instead of forwarded. The fix also requires exactly one `Host` header, rejects malformed header lines, and checks an absolute-form request target against the SNI.

### Workarounds
Before upgrading, avoid allowlisting hostnames on shared infrastructure for sandboxes that run untrusted code, or disable networking for those sandboxes.

### References
- Related advisory: [GHSA-3mpp-52gc-935r](https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/security/advisories/GHSA-3mpp-52gc-935r)

cwes.name: Improper Validation of Syntactic Correctness of Input

summary: Guest-controlled symlinks in msb copy allow arbitrary file write on the host
description:
### Summary
`msb copy` from a sandbox to the host recreated symlinks reported by the guest without validating their targets, and wrote file contents through symlinks that already existed at the destination. Code running inside a sandbox could arrange its filesystem so that copying a directory out of the sandbox wrote attacker-controlled content to a host path outside the copy destination, with the permissions of the user running `msb copy`.

### Impact
An attacker who can execute code inside a sandbox can overwrite arbitrary files on the host that the invoking user can write to, once that user or an automated job copies data out of the sandbox. Targets such as shell startup files, SSH `authorized_keys`, or git hooks can turn the file write into code execution on the host. If `msb copy` runs under a privileged account, the impact extends to whatever that account can write.

No special sandbox configuration is required. In the reported scenario the write happens when a guest-controlled directory is copied to the same host destination more than once.

### Affected configurations
The issue affects versions 0.5.3 through 0.6.6 when `msb copy` is used to copy files from a sandbox that ran untrusted code to the host.

This covers the `msb` CLI however it was installed, including the standalone installer, the `microsandbox-cli` crate, and the npm and pip packages, which ship the CLI.

### Details
During copy-out, the symlink target string returned by the guest was passed directly to the host `symlink` call, with no check for absolute paths or `..` components. Only the location of the link was confined to the destination. File contents were then written with a create-and-truncate open that follows symlinks, so a later copy of a regular file with the same name was written to the link's target instead.

### Patches
Fixed in 0.6.7. Copy-out now pins the destination root, re-anchors absolute guest symlink targets inside the copy tree, rejects targets that would leave it, and no longer follows symlinks beneath the destination when writing files.

### Workarounds
Before upgrading, avoid running `msb copy` out of sandboxes that ran untrusted code. If you must, copy into a new empty directory each time and check the result for symlinks before using it.

cwes.name: Improper Link Resolution Before File Access

summary: IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses bypass DNS rebind protection
description:
## Summary

Before v0.6.3, DNS rebind protection checked AAAA answers against native IPv6 private ranges but did not check the embedded IPv4 address in an IPv4-mapped IPv6 answer. An answer such as `::ffff:169.254.169.254` could pass the filter and enter the resolved-hostname pin cache.

## Impact

In an environment where IPv4-mapped IPv6 destinations are connectable, a workload running inside a network-enabled sandbox could reach a restricted private, loopback, link-local, or metadata IPv4 endpoint through its mapped address. The same DNS answer could satisfy the resolved-hostname pin used by domain-scoped secret substitution. Secret substitution also depends on the configured secret policy and hostname checks; the report did not demonstrate secret disclosure in a live sandbox.

## Affected versions

The affected network code shipped in v0.4.0 through v0.6.2 of the Rust SDK, CLI, Python SDK, and Node SDK, and in v0.5.0 through v0.6.2 of the Go SDK. All listed packages are fixed in v0.6.3.

## Fix

[PR #1083](https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/pull/1083) checks the embedded IPv4 address during DNS rebind filtering and normalizes mapped addresses for network policy classification, CIDR matching, and resolved-hostname pin insertion and lookup. It adds regression tests for mapped private and metadata addresses. The fix shipped in [v0.6.3](https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/releases/tag/v0.6.3) on July 4, 2026.

## Credit

Reported by [Leroy H. Mason (@LHMisme420)](https://github.com/LHMisme420).

summary: Secret values exposed in world-readable process arguments
description:
### Summary
When a sandbox was started, the `msb` sandbox process received its network configuration and environment variables as command-line arguments. Process arguments are visible to other local users through `ps` and, on Linux, through `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`. The network configuration includes the real values of configured secrets, so any local user on the host could read those values for as long as the sandbox was running.

### Impact
Local disclosure of secrets and environment values to other users or processes on the same host. No privileges and no code execution inside the sandbox are required; the values can be read from the host process list.

This matters most on shared or multi-tenant hosts, CI runners, and machines that run other untrusted software alongside microsandbox.

### Affected configurations
The issue affects versions 0.3.0 through 0.5.8 when both of the following are true:

- a sandbox is started with configured secrets, or with sensitive values in its environment
- other local users or untrusted processes on the host can list processes

Versions before 0.3.0 have not been assessed.

### Patches
Fixed in 0.5.10 by [#1006](https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/pull/1006). The sandbox configuration, including the network configuration and environment, is now passed to the sandbox process over an inherited file descriptor instead of on the command line.

### Workarounds
Before upgrading, run sandboxes that use secrets only on hosts where other users cannot list your processes, or restrict process visibility, for example by mounting `/proc` with `hidepid=2` on Linux. Consider rotating secrets that were used with affected versions on shared hosts.

cwes.name: Invocation of Process Using Visible Sensitive Information

summary: Snapshot Import Symlink Traversal Arbitrary File Write
description:
### Summary
`msb snapshot import` and the SDK snapshot import APIs (Rust, Node.js, Python, Go) did not validate tar entry types when unpacking a snapshot archive. A crafted archive containing a symlink entry followed by a regular file entry whose path passes through that symlink could write attacker-controlled files outside the intended import destination, with the permissions of the user running the import.

### Impact
An attacker who can get a user or an automated pipeline to import a malicious snapshot archive can write arbitrary content to any path that user can write to. This can be used to:

- overwrite files such as `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` or shell startup files to gain persistence or code execution as that user
- corrupt application or sandbox data to cause denial of service

The write happens during extraction, before the snapshot manifest is checked, so it succeeds even when the import itself exits with an error.

Exploitation requires the victim to import an archive supplied by the attacker.

### Affected configurations
The issue affects versions 0.4.4 through 0.5.7 when a snapshot archive from an untrusted source is imported through any of:

- the `msb snapshot import` CLI command
- the snapshot import API in the Rust crate or the Node.js, Python, or Go SDKs (the Go SDK from 0.5.0, its first release)

Both plain `.tar` and `.tar.zst` archives were affected.

### Details
`unpack_archive()` in `crates/microsandbox/lib/snapshot/archive.rs` rejected entries with absolute paths or `..` components, but never inspected the entry type or link target before calling `entry.unpack()`. A symlink entry at a relative path (for example `snap/link`) pointing to a location outside the import root, followed by a regular file entry at `snap/link/<name>`, passes both path checks. When the second entry is unpacked the OS follows the symlink and the file lands outside the destination.

### Patches
Fixed in 0.5.8 by [#998](https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/pull/998). Snapshot and cache archive contents are now staged in a temporary directory, entries that are not regular files or directories are rejected, and nothing is promoted to its final location until every snapshot manifest verifies.

Upgrade to 0.5.8 or later. The npm package did not ship a 0.5.8 release, so npm users should upgrade to 0.5.10 or later.

### Workarounds
On affected versions, only import snapshot archives from sources you trust. To inspect an archive first, list its entries (for example with `tar -tvf`) and do not import it if it contains symlinks, hard links, or device entries.

summary: Microsandbox domain deny rule bypass via direct-IP TLS connection
description:
### Summary
Microsandbox domain and suffix deny rules could be bypassed for TLS traffic when default egress was set to allow. A process in the sandbox could connect directly to an IP address and send a TLS SNI matching the denied hostname, without first resolving it through the sandbox DNS path, and the connection was allowed.

Allow and deny rules shared one domain matching helper. For SNI-based `Destination::Domain` and `Destination::DomainSuffix` checks, it required both a hostname match and a prior DNS-cache binding between the destination IP and that hostname. That binding is correct for allow rules, since it stops a guest from spoofing SNI for an unrelated IP. For deny rules it meant a missing binding made the rule a non-match, so evaluation fell through to `default_egress: Allow`.

### Impact
An attacker who can execute code inside a sandbox could open TLS connections to a domain the operator explicitly denied. This weakens domain blocklists used to block exfiltration destinations, internal services reachable by IP, or policy-controlled SaaS endpoints.

This is not a host escape and does not by itself grant code execution outside the sandbox.

### Affected configurations
The issue affects versions before 0.5.0 when all of the following are true:

- the sandbox uses permissive default egress (`--net-default allow`);
- the policy relies on a domain or suffix deny rule, such as `deny@evil.com` or `deny@*.evil.com`;
- untrusted or attacker-controlled code can run inside the sandbox and connect directly to an IP address that serves the denied hostname over TLS.

Sandboxes using default-deny egress with hostname allow rules are not affected by this issue, because allow rules already required the DNS-cache binding.

### Patches
Upgrade to 0.5.1 or later (0.5.0 where available).

- 0.5.0 makes SNI domain matching action-aware: deny rules match on the SNI alone, while allow rules still require the DNS-cache binding.
- 0.5.0 was not published to npm and was yanked from crates.io, so npm and Rust users should use 0.5.1.

### Workarounds
If you cannot upgrade, use default-deny egress with explicit allow rules instead of relying on domain deny rules.

### References
- Fix: #782
- v0.5.0 release: https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/releases/tag/v0.5.0
